The operational municipal solid waste 
management policy focuses on identifying 
waste generation behavior across multiple 
levels in mega cities, a case study
Hamed Alimoradiyan1,2, Ahmad Hajinezhad1*, Hossein Yousefi1 and Mario Giampietro2
Discover Sustainability
Abstract
The results of an effort to create a thorough framework that efficiently arranges 
and combines quantitative data characterizing the performance of Urban Waste 
Management Systems (UWMS) across a range of scales and dimensions are 
presented in this study. The theory of metabolic networks and the Multi-Scale 
Integrated Analysis of Societal and Ecosystem Metabolism (MuSIASEM) serve as the 
foundation for the developed framework. According to this conceptualization, the 
UWMS functions as an organ within a socio-ecological system, controlling urban 
metabolism and providing resources and capacity for regional sinks within the larger 
waste management system. This study demonstrates how impact indicators other 
than income, like district size, financial types, and economic activity, can be identified 
as explanatory variables when employing Python software and the K-means method 
to analyze MSW generation behavior across multiple organizational levels. The 
findings reveal significant disparities in waste generation across Tehran, the capital 
city of Iran. Waste density varied from 25 to 861 kg/ha, with particularly high values 
in three emerging districts. Developing areas exhibited higher waste production due 
to increased consumption facilities for different social elements. Moreover, developed 
regions produce more waste per person, attributed to higher input (consumption) 
and consequently higher waste generation. Furthermore, a waste estimation analysis 
was conducted to systematically assess and compute the volume and types of waste 
generated within specific regions. These insights contribute to optimizing waste 
management strategies, offering data-driven guidance for policymakers and urban 
planners to enhance sustainability and efficiency in waste management systems.
Keywords  Municipal waste management, Waste metabolic networks, Impact 
indicator, Tehran city

1  Introduction
The third millennium has seen a global urbanization phenomenon, making municipal 
solid waste management a top priority for all governments worldwide, developed or 
developing [31]. A Municipal Solid Waste Management System (MSWMS) is a complex 
framework that manages the disposal, treatment, and recycling of solid waste generated 
by a municipality [2]. Evaluating its performance entails taking into account a variety 
of analytical factors at different stages of operation. This is important because there is 
a chance that poor waste management will give rise to problems with the environment, 
the economy, and public health, which could spark social unrest [7, 29].
Kyoto City is internationally recognized for its highly structured and community-
driven waste management system, which integrates waste separation, advanced recy­
cling mechanisms, and circular economy principles. The city has successfully reduced 
landfill dependency through a combination of strict waste sorting policies, public par­
ticipation, and government-supported recycling initiatives. Unlike Tehran, where public 
engagement in waste separation remains low, Kyoto has achieved high citizen compli­
ance with waste policies, facilitated by clear guidelines, economic incentives, and educa­
tional campaigns [6].
Sikkim, a mountainous state in India, faces waste management challenges shaped by 
its unique geography and limited infrastructure. Unlike Kyoto, where advanced tech­
nologies and structured policies define waste handling, Sikkim’s Himalayan smart cities 
operate under constraints such as rugged terrain, low population density, and restricted 
waste transportation options. These factors make traditional large-scale waste process­
ing facilities impractical. Instead, localized and decentralized waste management strate­
gies, such as on-site composting, small-scale recycling units, and community-led waste 
programs, have been implemented to reduce environmental impact [34].
The control of production, storage, collection, transportation, processing, and disposal 
of solid waste materials in compliance with the highest standards of hygiene, econom­
ics, resource conservation, aesthetics, and other environmental requirements is known 
as waste management In fact, waste management is a broad field that touches on many 
other disciplines, and a number of factors, such as public interest, affect how effective it 
is [16, 46].
The quality and quantity of materials are influenced by economic variables, urban set­
ting, land uses, cultural factors, and population density [27, 39]; consequently, numer­
ous components are engaged in the system for waste management. The aforementioned 
information indicates that the urban waste management system's design is a delicate and 
unique issue that cannot be resolved in a single solution or piecemeal fashion. In addi­
tion to the implementation of diverse management concepts and strategies, a compre­
hensive and forward-thinking approach is necessary to address the challenges of waste 
management [41].
The Kepner-Tregoe (K-T) method is a hierarchical approach to strategic planning and 
decision-making that may prove beneficial to waste management sector decision-mak­
ers. The K-T method offers a systematic framework for the examination and resolution 
of intricate issues, rendering it highly suitable for contexts involving the consideration 
of numerous variables, such as waste management. Leaders can enhance sustainability, 
efficiency, and environmental responsibility in waste management practices through 
the implementation of a systematic approach that includes situation appraisal, problem

regarding design processes and strategic planning in municipal waste management are 
inextricably linked. While design processes establish the particular methods and systems 
employed to accomplish those objectives, strategic decisions dictate the overarching tra­
jectory and targets of waste management endeavors. The design group approach, which 
is frequently abbreviated as "fundamental design methodology" and was introduced by 
the School of Mechanics at MIT University, places significant emphasis on the value of 
principled design when it comes to tackling intricate engineering challenges [13].
The goal (needs) and the strategy (activity), both of which have a hierarchical struc­

tegic planning [17, 36]. The design relationship is used to show how the two objective 
spaces relate to one another. The preparation and extraction of pertinent strategies has 
accounted for the majority of the work done with this approach [22, 26, 28].
Sanitary landfills equipped with environmental controls are used to dispose of waste. 
While recycling and composting systems are also becoming more and more popular 
worldwide, open dumping accounts for about 27% of trash disposal [40]. Cities like Mex­
ico City, Mexico, and Rosario, Argentina compost more than 10% of waste, while Mon­
tevideo, Uruguay, Bogotá, and Medellín, Colombia, recycle more than 15% of waste [25].
Waste management is usually a local responsibility, and about 70% of countries have 
facilities in place for creating regional required treatments. For the management of solid 
waste, laws and regulations have been passed in two thirds of the countries. Public enti­
ties provide at least half of the services, which include primary garbage collection, treat­
ment, and disposal. Approximately one-third of the services are provided through public 
partnerships [33].
It is important to remember that creating a waste management strategy is only one of 
several strategic planning rings. The creation, application, and assessment of strategies 
are all included in strategic planning [9, 15, 21]. In the field of waste management, indi­
cators are presented, and the goal function—or functions—that are chosen with the help 
of these indicators are those that reduce the disparity in waste management between the 
waste center locations in Tehran Municipality [35, 38].
The first approaches to using system-analysis methods to enhance waste management 
decision-making date back to 1970. In particular, system engineering models and sys­
tem assessments are the two groups that are most readily distinguished [10]. Various 
authors have proposed distinct classifications by dividing the techniques according to 
the selected strategy [4, 12, 30].
System assessments of waste management commonly employ a number of fundamen­
tal methodologies to evaluate the sustainability, effectiveness, and efficiency of waste 
management systems. The aforementioned methodologies comprise a multitude of 
waste management facets, such as production, collection, conveyance, treatment, recy­
cling, and disposal [1, 5, 14, 24, 32].
Similar challenges are observed in other global cities, such as Addis Ababa, Ethiopia’s 
capital, that faces persistent waste management challenges due to insufficient collection 
systems, a lack of waste treatment facilities, and heavy reliance on open dumping. The 
city’s primary landfill, Koshe, gained international attention after a tragic landslide in 
2017, underscoring the severe environmental and human risks associated with unregu­
lated waste disposal. Unlike Tehran, where formal waste collection covers a significant

networks. Lessons from Addis Ababa emphasize the importance of waste treatment 
diversification and landfill risk mitigation, which Tehran can consider as it evaluates 
alternatives to landfill dependency [43].
Jakarta, the capital of Indonesia, exhibits a dual waste management system dominated 
by both formal waste collection services and an extensive informal recycling sector. 
Unlike Tehran, where formal municipal services play the primary role, Jakarta heavily 
depends on waste pickers, known as pemulung, who manually collect and sort recy­
clable materials from households and landfills. While this system provides a means of 
income for thousands of low-income individuals, it also leads to inefficiencies in waste 
sorting and recycling, as informal operations lack regulatory oversight. Moreover, Jakar­
ta’s massive population generates around 7000 tons of waste per day, and its reliance on 
the Bantar Gebang landfill—one of the largest in Southeast Asia—raises concerns about 
long-term waste sustainability. Jakarta’s case highlights the importance of integrating 
informal waste workers into a regulated system, something Tehran has struggled with 
due to socio-economic constraints and policy gaps. Studying Jakarta’s mixed approach 
can offer insights into how Tehran might balance formal municipal waste services with 
potential informal sector contributions [42].
Moreover, São Paulo, Brazil’s largest city, faces waste management disparities across its 
districts, where wealthier areas benefit from more advanced recycling and collection ser­
vices while lower-income neighborhoods struggle with inefficient waste disposal. Unlike 
Tehran, which primarily relies on landfilling, São Paulo has actively invested in waste-
to-energy (WtE) solutions, converting waste into electricity to reduce landfill depen­
dency. The city has also implemented progressive policies promoting circular economy 
practices, including extended producer responsibility (EPR) programs that place waste 
reduction accountability on manufacturers. However, São Paulo still faces challenges 
in fully transitioning away from landfills, as regulatory barriers and public resistance to 
new waste management infrastructure persist. Tehran can learn from São Paulo’s policy-
driven approach to sustainable waste management, particularly in terms of integrating 
WtE technologies and promoting extended producer responsibility in waste governance.
However, Tehran's waste management landscape presents distinct complexities. 
Unlike cities with well-integrated waste-to-energy initiatives, Tehran's system remains 
highly dependent on landfills, with limited recycling infrastructure and public participa­
tion. Additionally, socio-economic factors, consumption patterns, and urban planning 
deficiencies contribute to uneven waste generation across districts. Addressing these 
challenges requires a multi-faceted approach that incorporates data-driven methodolo­
gies, technological interventions, and policy reforms. This imbalance highlights the need 
for an integrated and sustainable waste management framework that not only optimizes 
waste flow but also accounts for the interconnections between socio-economic, envi­
ronmental, and technological dimensions, which is where the Multi-Scale Integrated 
Analysis of Societal and Ecosystem Metabolism (MuSIASEM) approach becomes valu­
able. The MuSIASEM framework provides a multi-level, systemic approach to analyzing 
urban waste management by linking socio-economic processes (such as consumption

By examining global case studies and leveraging quantitative tools such as Python-

framework for optimizing Tehran’s waste management system. This comparative per­
spective will enhance the understanding of urban waste dynamics and support the for­

This study presents the results of a novel approach to the analysis of MSW genera­
tion statistics in Tehran. The purpose of this study is to investigate the variables that 
affect the production of Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) in households and to ascertain 
the ways in which these variables affect various socioeconomic strata. The principal aim 
is to furnish a strong informational underpinning for the development of MSW manage­
ment policy in the swiftly expanding urban regions of Iran. The research will aid in the 
improvement of waste management practices, the reduction of environmental impacts, 
and the enhancement of the quality of life for urban residents by providing a solid infor­
mational foundation for MSW management policy in Iran's rapidly expanding metro­
politan areas. In addition, a study on generation forecasting has been carried out to 
support relevant policy makers and offer a broad outlook on the generation of waste in 
the future. Establishing a solid informational foundation for MSW executive policies in 
Iran's quickly growing urban areas is the primary objective of this research.
2  Materials and methods
2.1  Research framework
MuSIASEM (Multi-Scale Integrated Analysis of Societal and Ecosystem Metabolism) is 
a methodological framework used in sustainability science to analyze socio-ecological 
systems across multiple scales, from local to global. It examines information, material, 
and energy flows within and between ecosystems and human societies, highlighting their 
interdependencies. MuSIASEM emphasizes the need for integrated rather than isolated 
analysis of social and ecological systems to capture complex feedback loops influencing 
sustainability. It often uses quantitative models—ranging from simple to complex—to 
assess these flows. In municipal waste management, MuSIASEM can help identify inef­
ficiencies, environmental impacts, and opportunities for improvement, while also evalu­
ating broader socio-economic and ecological effects of different policies. The approach 
is grounded in metabolic network theory and integrated accounting principles. [18–20].
Within the MuSIASEM framework, a specialized grammar can be developed for 
municipal waste management to analyze energy, material, and information flows and 
assess the impacts of various interventions on sustainability. This grammar defines key 
elements, variables, and relationships unique to waste metabolism, which differs from 
grammars for inputs like food, energy, and water. In this context, society is viewed as the 
"source" of waste, and the environment becomes the "consumer."
The waste management system processes solid, liquid, and gaseous waste before 
release into the environment. Its effectiveness is judged by its ability to:
(i)	Manage waste without disrupting daily life;
(ii)	Break down waste into manageable components;
(iii)	 Recover usable materials; and
(iv)	 Minimize environmental and health impacts.

The framework integrates multidisciplinary indicators and classifies them according to 
three sustainability criteria:
1.	 Feasibility– external constraints beyond system control (e.g., environmental limits, 
regulations);
2.	 Viability– internal factors within system control (e.g., economic or technical 
parameters);
3.	 Desirability– societal values and normative goals. [11]
It is concluded that the MuSIASEM framework was chosen for its ability to link socio-
economic activities with environmental constraints, making it particularly useful for 
analyzing waste metabolism in rapidly urbanizing cities like Tehran. By considering 
different scales—from district-level waste production to city-wide waste processing 
capacities—MuSIASEM enables a systemic understanding of metabolic inefficiencies 
and highlights potential intervention points [3]. The use of metabolic network model­
ing allows for a quantitative representation of waste flows, identifying bottlenecks in 
collection, treatment, and recycling. This approach is complemented by Python-based 
analytics and K-means clustering, which facilitate pattern recognition in waste genera­
tion behaviors, enabling classification of districts based on their socio-economic and 
consumption profiles. The combination of these methods ensures both qualitative depth 
and quantitative precision, enhancing the robustness of the analysis.
2.2  Case study
The Iranian city of Tehran is the subject of the case study. Tehran, the capital of Iran, is 
situated between 35 degrees and 31 min to 35° and 58 min north latitude and 51° and 
4 min to 51° and 48 min east longitude. The city is roughly 838 square kilometers in size 
[8]. The central, northern, and northeastern regions of Tehran are encompassed by the 
southern highlands of Alborz, which also encircle the city from the western side of the 
Saujblag plain, the southern side of the Ray and Bibi Shahrabano mountains, and the 
plains that lead to the salt desert. Tehran is divided into 22 urban areas, with district 4 
being the largest at 137 square kilometers and the smallest at 88.2 square kilometers, 
according to the most recent urban classification (district 18). Figure 2 shows the bound­
aries of different districts of Tehran including of the related area.
The Iranian city of Tehran is the subject of this case study. As the capital of Iran, Teh­
ran covers an area of approximately 730 square kilometers, according to the most recent 
urban classification. The city is surrounded by the Alborz mountain range in the north 
and northeast, while the western boundary extends to the Saujblag plain, and the south­

divided into 22 urban districts, with district 4 being the largest (137 square kilometers) 
and district 18 being the smallest (88.2 square kilometers). Additionally, Tehran has a

2.3  Data analysis
The flow-fund model is a key component of the MuSIASEM (Multi-Scale Integrated 
Analysis of Societal and Ecosystem Metabolism) methodology. In MuSIASEM, the

flow-fund model is used to represent the flows of energy, materials, and information 
within socio-ecological systems.
As illustrated in Fig.  1, the flow-fund model postulates a relationship between the 
flows that are produced and consumed (inputs and outputs) and the structural elements 
(funds) that make up the nodes (specified at a lower hierarchical level of analysis) (out­
puts). As a result, as illustrated in Fig. 1, it is required to define: I the lower-level fund 
elements' size or capacity (an extensive variable); and (ii) their metabolic rate or flow 
throughput per unit of fund (an intensive variable). Aside from these epistemological 
issues, there are two different methods for defining a network's properties: top-down 
and bottom-up. Conversely, the internal perspective, or bottom-up definition, starts 
with the local scale conversion processes and works its way up to the node's metabolic 
capacity. The characteristics and relative composition of the structural elements that 
make up the node are examined (metabolic rate or technical coefficients of each of these 
elements). A forced relation of congruence between the top-down definition, which pro­
vides a functional description at the interface of levels n and n-1, and the bottom-up 
definition, which provides a structural description at the interface of levels n-1 and n-2, 
is therefore necessary for a metabolic network to function properly.

urban waste management systems (UWMS) in Tehran city.
Figure 2 highlights three main elements depicted: transportation and disposal at level 
n, local stations for import/export at level n-1, and collection at level n-2. These ele­
ments illustrate the flow of waste within the urban waste management system, with

These items are crucial for understanding the boundaries of the waste management sys­

It suggests that different combinations of functional nodes can achieve the same phases,

plexity and flexibility of waste management systems, where multiple pathways and 
technologies can be employed to achieve similar outcomes. It is concluded that Fig. 2 
provides insights into the structure and operation of urban waste management systems, 
emphasizing the need to understand both internal and external flows of waste and the

2.4  Clustering
K-means clustering is a widely used unsupervised machine learning algorithm that 
groups data based on similarities, offering valuable applications in municipal waste 
management to improve efficiency and resource allocation. It can group similar waste 
types (e.g., organic, recyclable, hazardous) based on characteristics like composition and 
recyclability, enabling more effective sorting and disposal strategies. It also helps opti­
mize waste collection routes by clustering areas with similar waste generation patterns, 
reducing fuel use, emissions, and collection time. Additionally, K-means can analyze 
historical data to predict future waste generation trends influenced by factors like sea­
sonality and population growth, aiding in infrastructure planning. It can also segment 
households and businesses by recycling behavior, supporting targeted outreach to boost 
recycling rates. Python’s flexibility and ease of use make it an ideal tool for implementing 
K-means, offering robust data preprocessing, visualization, and integration capabilities, 
even for novice users [23].

2.5  Forecasting
The application of Exponential Smoothing with a Trend in waste estimation analysis 
denotes the implementation of a statistical technique utilized to quantify and examine 
the production, structure, and administration of waste materials within a designated 
region or system. This analytical methodology is of the utmost importance for numerous 
objectives, such as policy formulation, resource optimization, and environmental man­
agement. Exponential Smoothing with a Trend is a time series forecasting technique that 
integrates a trend component to capture potential future patterns in addition to histori­
cal data points. This method facilitates the correlation between resource consumption 
parameters and the behavior of individuals in terms of Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) 
generation, as it relates to waste estimation. In this investigation, the Independent Vari­
ables (IFs) are classified according to their financial and district development charac­
teristics. The variables in question are presumed to have been obtained from the latest 
publishing database of the Tehran municipality, thereby furnishing the analysis with cur­
rent and pertinent information. Through the utilization of pertinent IFs and Exponential 
Smoothing with a Trend, the analysis endeavors to unveil patterns and trends in MSW 
generation. This data may provide decision-makers and planners with valuable insights 
into the intricacies of waste generation in various districts, taking into consideration 
their financial characteristics and levels of development. It is worth noting that exponen­
tial smoothing placed the greatest emphasis on the most recent observations [44]. There 
is a way to adjust exponential smoothing to trends that this is also known as Double

increased waste production. The significance of waste estimation analysis in facilitating 
informed decision-making and promoting sustainable waste management is emphasized 
by the recognition of this recurring annual pattern.
By virtue of its analytical framework, this method is indispensable for developing 
waste management strategies that are resilient to shifting patterns, environmentally con­
scious, and sustainable in the long run.

3  Discussions and recommendations
This study explores how municipal solid waste (MSW) generation in Tehran correlates 
with development levels of districts, developed (District 1), developing (District 5), and 
underdeveloped (District 17), highlighting that household and district-level income 
significantly influence MSW output, with higher household income leading to greater 
waste. Indigenous populations also contribute notably to increased organic waste due 
to dietary habits. The development status of a district emerges as the strongest predic­
tor of MSW generation patterns, and functional units within similar development tiers 
show clustering tendencies. However, intra-organizational variations and contextual 
shifts influence behavior across spatial levels, making linear models insufficient. Instead, 
multidimensional approaches using vector, matrix, and tensor representations are rec­
ommended to capture the complex, overlapping influences. The study emphasizes that 
absolute income cannot be generalized across all scales, and effect size analysis requires 
larger samples for deeper insights. By comparing Tehran with São Paulo and Kyoto, the 
study illustrates how MSW patterns reflect broader socio-economic, governance, and 
infrastructural differences, advocating for integrated waste management strategies that 
combine policy reform, public engagement, and technological innovation.
4  Conclusions
With rapid urbanization and rising consumption, managing municipal solid waste 
(MSW) has become increasingly complex. This study employs a framework based on 
MuSIASEM and metabolic network theory to analyze Urban Waste Management Sys­
tems (UWMS) across multiple scales. It conceptualizes the UWMS not just as a func­
tional entity but as a key regulatory component of socio-ecological systems, acting as a 
supplier that manages waste flows and local sink capacities.
The study aims to build a knowledge base for formulating effective MSW policies, 
especially in fast-growing urban areas of developing countries. It highlights income 
as a major determinant of MSW generation, influencing waste output at individual to 
national levels. Other influential factors include district size, economic activity, and 
funding mechanisms. Using computational tools like Python and K-means clustering, 
the analysis enhances data accuracy and informs more targeted, effective policies. Teh­
ran, Iran, serves as the case study due to its dynamic urban context. Waste estimation—
predicting waste volume and composition over time—is central to strategic planning 
and sustainable resource management. Ultimately, MSW generation does not follow a 
linear pattern. Instead, it is shaped by multiple interdependent variables at various spa­
tial levels. This complexity necessitates informed, nuanced decision-making by policy 
committees to address urban waste challenges effectively.
This study provides a robust framework for urban waste metabolism analysis, but 
future research should explore:
 	•
Replication of the MuSIASEM Approach in Different Urban Contexts– Applying this 
methodology to cities with different cultural, economic, and governance structures 
could test its adaptability and scalability.
 	•
Longitudinal Studies on Policy Implementation– Evaluating the long-term impact 
of policy interventions informed by this study’s findings could guide effective 
governance strategies.

Abstract: The results of an effort to create a thorough framework that efficiently arranges and combines quantitative data characterizing the performance of Urban Waste Management Systems (UWMS) across a range of scales and dimensions are presented in this study. The theory of metabolic networks and the Multi-Scale Integrated Analysis of Societal and Ecosystem Metabolism (MuSIASEM) serve as the foundation for the developed framework. According to this conceptualization, the UWMS functions as an organ within a socio-ecological system, controlling urban metabolism and providing resources and capacity for regional sinks within the larger waste management system. This study demonstrates how impact indicators other than income, like district size, financial types, and economic activity, can be identified as explanatory variables when employing Python software and the K-means method to analyze MSW generation behavior across multiple organizational levels. The findings reveal significant disparities in waste generation across Tehran, the capital city of Iran. Waste density varied from 25 to 861 kg/ha, with particularly high values in three emerging districts. Developing areas exhibited higher waste production due to increased consumption facilities for different social elements. Moreover, developed regions produce more waste per person, attributed to higher input (consumption) and consequently higher waste generation. Furthermore, a waste estimation analysis was conducted to systematically assess and compute the volume and types of waste generated within specific regions. These insights contribute to optimizing waste management strategies, offering data-driven guidance for policymakers and urban planners to enhance sustainability and efficiency in waste management systems.
